{{Short description|Numerals used in Ancient Egypt}}
{{Numeral systems}}
{{Contains special characters}}
The system of ancient '''Egyptian numerals''' was used in [[Ancient Egypt]] from around 3000 BC<ref>{{cite web|title=Egyptian numerals|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Egyptian_numerals/|website=MacTutor - School of Mathematics and Statistics|publisher=University of St. Andrews|access-date=January 12, 2023}}</ref> until the early first millennium AD. It was a system of numeration based on multiples of ten, often rounded off to the higher power, written in [[Egyptian hieroglyph|hieroglyph]]s. 

The Egyptians had no concept of a [[positional notation]] such as the [[Decimal|decimal system]].<ref>"The Story of Numbers" by John McLeish</ref> The [[hieratic]] form of numerals stressed an exact finite series notation, ciphered one-to-one onto the Egyptian alphabet.{{fact|date=December 2020}}

==Digits and numbers==
The following hieroglyphs were used to denote [[Exponentiation|powers]] of ten:
<gallery class="center">
Hiero-numeral_1.jpg|1 <br />Z15<br />𓏤<br /> Single stroke
Hiero-numeral_10.jpg|10 <br />V20<br /> 𓎆<br /> Cattle [[Hobble (device)|hobble]]
Hiero-numeral_100.jpg|100 <br />V1<br /> 𓍢<br /> Coil of [[rope]]
Hiero-numeral_1 000.jpg|1,000 <br />M12<br /> 𓆼<br /> [[Nymphaea lotus|Water lily]]<br/>(also called lotus)
Hiero-numeral_10 000.jpg|10,000 <br /> D50<br /> 𓂭<br /> Bent finger
Hiero-numeral_100 000.jpg|100,000 <br /> I8<br /> 𓆐<br /> Tadpole
Hiero-numeral_1 000 000.jpg|1,000,000 <br /> C11<br /> 𓁨<br /> [[Heh (god)|Heh]]<ref>[[Uta Merzbach|Merzbach, Uta C.]], and Carl B. Boyer. A History of Mathematics. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley, 2011, p. 10</ref>
</gallery>

Multiples of these values were expressed by repeating the symbol as many times as needed. For instance, a stone carving from [[Karnak]] shows the number 4,622 as:
{| align="center"
|<hiero>M12-M12-M12-M12-!-V1*V1*V1:V1*V1*V1-!-V20-V20-Z1-Z1</hiero>
|}

Egyptian hieroglyphs could be written in [[Bi-directional text|both directions]] (and even vertically). In this example the symbols decrease in value from top to bottom and from left to right. On the original stone carving, it is right-to-left, and the signs are thus reversed.{{fact|date=December 2020}}

== Zero ==
There was no symbol or concept of [[0|zero]] as a placeholder in Egyptian numeration and zero was not used in calculations.{{sfn|Hoffmann|2024}} The symbol [[nefer|nfr]]:<hiero>
F35
</hiero>meaning "good", "complete", "beautiful" served two similar, albeit non-mathematical, purposes:{{sfn | Joseph | 2011 | p=86}}
* in a papyrus listing the court expenses, {{circa|1740 [[Anno Domini|BC]]}}, it indicated a fulfilled balance;<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Gobets |first=Peter |url=https://brill.com/view/title/68384 |title=The Origin and Significance of Zero: An Interdisciplinary Perspective |last2=Lawrence Kuhn |first2=Robert |date=2024-03-11 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=978-90-04-69156-8 |pages=75 |doi=10.1163/9789004691568_007}}</ref>
* in setting marks for the [[Pyramid of Nyuserre|Nyuserre pyramid]] and [[Mastabat al-Fir'aun]], ''nfr'' is used to indicate the architectural baseline: height and depths are measured "above ''nfr''" or "below ''nfr''" respectively.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Arnold |first=Dieter |title=Building in Egypt: pharaonic stone masonry |date=1991 |publisher=Oxford university press |isbn=978-0-19-506350-9 |location=New York |pages=17}}</ref>
Mathematician and historian [[Carl Benjamin Boyer|Carl Boyer]], has claimed that a deed from [[Edfu]] contained a "zero concept" replacing the magnitude in geometry.{{sfn | Joseph | 2011 | p=87}} {{interlanguage link|Friedhelm Hoffmann|de}} however clarifies that in the Egyptian method of calculating area it was only in this later, Ptolemaic era document that it contained an explicit placeholder for no length on one side. He emphasizes that it was not merely the negation particle ''jw'' "𓂜" but ''jwty'', meaning "missing":<ref name=":0" /> <hiero>D35:G43</hiero>

==Fractions==
{{Main|Egyptian fraction}}

[[Rational number]]s could also be expressed, but only as sums of [[unit fraction]]s, ''i.e.'', sums of [[Reciprocal (mathematics)|reciprocal]]s of positive integers, except for {{frac|2|3}} and {{frac|3|4}}. The hieroglyph indicating a fraction looked like a mouth, which meant "part":
{| align="center"
|<hiero>D21</hiero>
|}
Fractions were written with this fractional [[Slash (punctuation)|solidus]], ''i.e.'', the [[numerator]] 1, and the positive [[denominator]] below. Thus, {{frac|3}} was written as:
{| align="center"
|<hiero>D21:Z1*Z1*Z1</hiero>
| <math>= \frac{1}{3}</math>
|}
Special symbols were used for {{frac|2}} and for the non-unit fractions {{frac|2|3}} and, less frequently, {{frac|3|4}}:
{| align="center"
|<hiero>Aa16</hiero>
|<math>= \frac{1}{2}</math>
|&nbsp;
|<hiero>D22</hiero>
|<math>= \frac{2}{3}</math>
|&nbsp;
|<hiero>D23</hiero>
|<math>= \frac{3}{4}</math>
|}
If the denominator became too large, the "mouth" was just placed over the beginning of the "denominator":
{| align="center"
|<hiero>D21:V1</hiero>
|<math>= \frac{1}{100}</math>
|}

==Written numbers==
As with most modern day languages, the ancient [[Egyptian language]] could also write out numerals as words phonetically, just like one can write ''thirty'' instead of "30" in [[English language|English]]. The word (''thirty''), for instance, was written as
{| align="center"
|<hiero>Aa15:D36-D58</hiero>
|}
while the numeral (''30'') was
{| align="center"
|<hiero>V20-V20-V20</hiero>
|}

This was, however, uncommon for most numbers other than one and the signs were used most of the time.{{sfn | Allen | 2014 | p=124}}

==Hieratic numerals==
As administrative and accounting texts were written on [[papyrus]] or  [[Ostracon|ostraca]],  rather than being carved into hard stone (as were hieroglyphic texts), the vast majority of texts employing the Egyptian numeral system utilize the [[hieratic]] script. Instances of numerals written in hieratic can be found as far back as the [[Early Dynastic Period of Egypt|Early Dynastic Period]]. The Old Kingdom [[Abusir Papyri]] are a particularly important corpus of texts that utilize hieratic numerals.{{fact|date=December 2020}}
[[File:A History Of Mathematical Notations Vol I - Egyptian numerals. Hieroglyphic, hieratic, and demotic numeral symbols. (This table, was compiled by Kurt Sethe.).png|thumb|A comparative chart of Egyptian numerals, including hieratic and demotic]]
Boyer proved 50 years ago{{When|date=December 2013}} that [[hieratic]] script used a different numeral system, using individual signs for the numbers 1 to 9, multiples of 10 from 10 to 90, the hundreds from 100 to 900, and the thousands from 1000 to 9000.  A large number like 9999 could thus be written with only four signs—combining the signs for 9000, 900, 90, and 9—as opposed to 36 hieroglyphs. Boyer saw the new hieratic numerals as ciphered, mapping one number onto one Egyptian letter for the first time in human history. Greeks adopted the new system, mapping their counting  numbers onto two of their alphabets, the Doric and Ionian.{{fact|date=December 2020}}

In the oldest hieratic texts the individual numerals were clearly written in a ciphered relationship to the Egyptian alphabet. But during the Old Kingdom a series of standardized writings had developed for sign-groups containing more than one numeral, repeated as [[Roman numerals]] practiced. However, repetition of the same numeral for each place-value was not allowed in the hieratic script. As the hieratic writing system developed over time, these sign-groups were further simplified for quick writing; this process continued into [[Demotic Egyptian|Demotic]], as well.{{fact|date=December 2020}}

Two famous mathematical papyri using hieratic script are the [[Moscow Mathematical Papyrus]] and the [[Rhind Mathematical Papyrus]].{{fact|date=December 2020}}

==Egyptian words for numbers==
The following table shows the reconstructed Middle Egyptian forms of the numerals (which are indicated by a preceding asterisk), the [[Egyptian transliteration|transliteration]] of the [[Egyptian hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] used to write them, and finally the [[Coptic language|Coptic]] numerals which descended from them and which give [[Egyptologist|Egyptologists]] clues as to the [[vowel|vocalism]] of the original Egyptian numbers. A breve (˘) in some reconstructed forms indicates a short vowel whose quality remains uncertain; the letter 'e' represents a vowel that was originally u or i (exact quality uncertain) but became e by Late Egyptian.{{fact|date=December 2020}}
